subject: HSS
overview: HSS 2 ('People Who Make a Difference') moves from family history to maps, government, economics and heroes, about 30 minutes a day. Each lesson: read or look at a source together, ask Who? What? When? Why?, have your child do the hands-on task (timeline, map, chart, role-play), and finish by having them explain the idea aloud in their own words. Keep the family history book, North America map and hero timeline going all year because later weeks build on them. Gather library biographies one to two weeks ahead, and preview the civil-rights and Japanese American incarceration material so you can explain unfairness calmly and simply.

weeks.prep: Calendar; old and new household objects or photos (rotary phone/smartphone, washboard/washing machine); 10 then-and-now picture cards; a Library of Congress photo of children around 1910 (loc.gov); 6 source cards (diary, textbook, photo, birth certificate, encyclopedia article, letter).
misconceptions: Thinking 'long ago' means last week: in history, long ago usually means before you (or your parents) were born.
Thinking a textbook is a primary source: a primary source was made at the time by someone who was there; a textbook is written later (secondary).

days.guide: Label yesterday, today and tomorrow on a calendar; write one thing done yesterday. Explain 'long ago' means before you were born.

questions.q: If today is Wednesday, what was yesterday?
questions.a: Tuesday.

questions.q: What does 'long ago' mean?
questions.a: A time far in the past, before you were born.

days.guide: Compare object pairs; sort 10 cards into long ago and today.

questions.q: Which is from long ago: a washboard or a washing machine?
questions.a: A washboard.

questions.q: How did people call each other long ago?
questions.a: With phones attached to the wall, like rotary phones, or by writing letters.

days.guide: Study an LOC photo of children around 1910. Ask Who? What? When? and record 3 clues of long ago.

questions.q: What clues show the photo is from long ago?
questions.a: Black-and-white photo, old-fashioned clothes (long dresses, caps, overalls), no modern cars or electronics.

questions.q: What is history?
questions.a: The story of what happened in the past.

days.guide: Teach primary (made at the time) vs. secondary (made later) sources; sort 6 items.

questions.q: Is a diary primary or secondary?
questions.a: Primary.

questions.q: Is a textbook primary or secondary?
questions.a: Secondary.

days.guide: Draw a long-ago and a today picture of a child's day; label 3 differences.

questions.q: Name one way children's lives were different long ago.
questions.a: Example: they did more chores by hand, walked to school, had no TV or computers.

weeks.assessment_key: Then/now sort: long ago - rotary phone, washboard, horse and buggy, oil lamp, typewriter; today - smartphone, washing machine, car, electric light, computer. Drawing labels 3 real differences (e.g., walked to school vs. ride in car; chores by hand vs. machines; played with simple toys vs. video games). Proficient = sort all correct + 3 labeled differences.

weeks.prep: Baby photos, adding-machine tape or long paper strip, markers; 6 morning-routine picture cards; a list of key family dates from a parent.
misconceptions: Putting events in the order remembered instead of the order they happened: check years.
Uneven spacing on the timeline: each year gets the same space.

days.guide: Order 6 morning-routine cards; talk through your life using before and after.

questions.q: What comes before eating breakfast?
questions.a: Example: waking up and getting dressed.

questions.q: What is a sequence?
questions.a: The order things happen.

days.guide: Ask a parent for birth date and 6 important events with years.

questions.q: What year were you born?
questions.a: Child's correct birth year.

questions.q: What is an event?
questions.a: Something that happens.

days.guide: Make a timeline with one mark per year; place each event.

questions.q: If you were born in 2018 and started kindergarten in 2023, how many years apart?
questions.a: 5 years.

questions.q: Which end of the timeline is the oldest event?
questions.a: The left (the beginning).

days.guide: Make a 4-box storyboard of one year and tell it in order.

questions.q: What happened first in your storyboard?
questions.a: Child's first event.

days.guide: Present the timeline using first, next, before, after, last.

questions.q: What happened right after you learned to walk?
questions.a: Answer from their timeline.

weeks.assessment_key: Timeline: equal marks for each year from birth year to now, 6 events placed in the correct year and order with drawings/photos; oral presentation uses first, next, before, after, last correctly. Proficient = all events correctly ordered and placed.

weeks.prep: 3-5 family artifacts (old photos, letters, recipe cards, tools), index cards for labels, a family document (copy of a birth certificate, old letter, report card), family history notebook.
misconceptions: Thinking an artifact must be very old or valuable: an artifact is any object people made or used that tells about their lives.
Placing grandparents below the child on the family tree: older generations go above (or at the roots).

days.guide: Collect 3-5 artifacts; set up a home museum; write labels (what it is, who used it).

questions.q: What is an artifact?
questions.a: An object made or used by people that tells about the past.

questions.q: What is an heirloom?
questions.a: A special object passed down in a family.

days.guide: Study one artifact with What? Who? When? Why important? and draw it.

questions.q: Who used this artifact?
questions.a: Answer based on family information.

days.guide: Look at a family document; record 3 facts it tells.

questions.q: What facts does a birth certificate tell?
questions.a: Name, birth date, birthplace, parents' names.

days.guide: Draw a family tree with names and birthplaces.

questions.q: What is an ancestor?
questions.a: A family member who lived before you, like a great-grandparent.

days.guide: Start the family history book with the tree and artifact pages.

questions.q: Who is your parent's parent?
questions.a: Your grandparent.

weeks.assessment_key: Family tree: child, parents, grandparents (great-grandparents if known) in correct generations with names and birthplaces. Artifact pages: each artifact drawn with answers to What is it? Who used it? When? Why important? Proficient = complete tree + 3 artifact pages.

weeks.prep: Interview question sheet, phone or recorder, Venn diagram paper; jacks, marbles or chalk for a long-ago game. Arrange a time with a grandparent or older relative.
misconceptions: Asking yes/no questions: open questions (What? How?) get better stories.
Thinking everything was worse long ago: some things were harder, some were simpler or fun; compare fairly.

days.guide: Write 6 interview questions for an older relative.

questions.q: Give an example of a good interview question.
questions.a: 'What games did you play when you were my age?'

days.guide: Conduct and record the interview; take notes in pictures and words.

questions.q: What is oral history?
questions.a: History told out loud by people who lived it.

days.guide: Make a Venn diagram comparing your life and theirs.

questions.q: What goes in the middle of a Venn diagram?
questions.a: Things that are the same for both.

questions.q: What does contrast mean?
questions.a: Tell how things are different.

days.guide: Play a long-ago game (jacks, hopscotch, marbles); write about it.

questions.q: How is this game different from games you play now?
questions.a: Uses simple objects, no screens or batteries.

days.guide: Add the interview and Venn diagram to the family history book.

questions.q: What did you learn about your relative's childhood?
questions.a: Specific fact from the interview.

weeks.assessment_key: Interview notes answer at least 5 of 6 questions (toys, school travel, food, chores, etc.). Venn diagram: at least 2 items in each circle and 2 in the middle (e.g., Grandma: walked to school, black-and-white TV; Me: tablet, car ride; Both: played tag, went to school). Proficient = complete notes + balanced Venn.

weeks.prep: Family history book, LOC photo of a one-room schoolhouse; cover materials; quiz cards (sources, timeline events).
misconceptions: Thinking all children long ago went to big schools: many rural children attended one-room schools.
Reading the book word for word when presenting: tell the story and point to pages.

days.guide: Compare a one-room schoolhouse photo with your learning space; list 4 differences.

questions.q: What was a one-room schoolhouse?
questions.a: A school where children of all ages learned together in one room with one teacher.

questions.q: Name a difference from today.
questions.a: Slates instead of paper/tablets, wood stove for heat, all ages together, walked far to school.

days.guide: Add a cover, a 'my life vs. my grandparent's' page and a family tradition page.

questions.q: What is a tradition?
questions.a: Something a family or group does again and again, often passed down.

days.guide: Practice telling your family story in 2 minutes.

questions.q: What will you tell first?
questions.a: Begins with family tree or earliest event.

days.guide: Present the family history book to relatives.

questions.q: What is the most interesting thing in your book?
questions.a: Child explains.

days.guide: Give the unit quiz.

questions.q: Is a photo taken in 1910 primary or secondary?
questions.a: Primary.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 quiz: Sources - primary: diary, photo, letter, birth certificate; secondary: textbook, encyclopedia. Timeline: orders 4 events by year correctly. Two ways life changed (e.g., phones/technology, how people travel, school, how chores are done). Presentation: 2 minutes, in order, uses book pages. Proficient = 80% quiz + clear presentation.

weeks.prep: Real compass; 3 sample maps (zoo, park, city) printed; sticky notes; a photo of a room taken from above (stand on a chair) and paper for maps.
misconceptions: Thinking north always means 'up' in the real world: north is a direction; on most maps it is at the top.
Confusing the legend with the title: the title tells what the map shows; the legend explains symbols.

days.guide: Compare an above photo of a room with a map; explain bird's-eye view.

questions.q: What is a bird's-eye view?
questions.a: Looking down from above, the way a bird would see.

questions.q: What is a map?
questions.a: A drawing of a place from above.

days.guide: Find title, legend, compass rose, scale and date on 3 maps; label with sticky notes.

questions.q: What does a legend (key) do?
questions.a: Explains what the symbols on the map mean.

questions.q: What does a scale show?
questions.a: How distance on the map compares to real distance.

days.guide: Use a compass to find north; label N, S, E, W walls; play a directions game.

questions.q: If you face north, what direction is behind you?
questions.a: South.

questions.q: Which direction does the sun rise?
questions.a: East.

days.guide: Draw a bedroom map with title, key and compass rose.

questions.q: What symbol did you use for your bed?
questions.a: Child's key symbol.

days.guide: Quiz on map elements and 4 directions.

questions.q: What are the four cardinal directions?
questions.a: North, south, east, west.

weeks.assessment_key: Room map: title, key with at least 4 symbols, compass rose (N, S, E, W), items drawn from above. Map-elements quiz: identifies title, legend/key, compass rose, scale and date; 4 direction questions answered correctly using the compass rose. Proficient = all elements + 4/4 directions.

weeks.prep: Grid paper; a printed online map of your neighborhood with a letter-number grid drawn on; colored pencils; a second community map for the quiz.
misconceptions: Naming the number before the letter: say the letter (column) first, then the number (row), like C3.
Confusing relative and absolute location: relative compares to other places ('next to the park'); absolute is exact (an address or grid square).

days.guide: Play 'grid battleship' on a 5x5 grid naming squares like C3.

questions.q: In C3, what does C stand for?
questions.a: The column (letter).

questions.q: What does 3 stand for?
questions.a: The row (number).

days.guide: Find home, school, park and store by grid square on a neighborhood map.

questions.q: What is a grid?
questions.a: Lines that cross to make squares so you can find places.

days.guide: Describe places using relative location.

questions.q: Describe where your house is using relative location.
questions.a: Example: 'My house is across from the park, south of the school.'

days.guide: Draw your own grid map with a key; list grid squares of 6 places.

questions.q: What is absolute location?
questions.a: The exact spot, like an address or grid square.

days.guide: Answer 8 grid questions on a new map.

questions.q: What is in square B2?
questions.a: Answer from map.

weeks.assessment_key: Grid map: neighborhood drawn on grid paper with a key and 6 places listed with correct grid squares. Quiz: 8 grid-location answers matching your map (check each letter-number pair). Proficient = 7-8 correct + complete map.

weeks.prep: Globe; blank North America outline map; colored pencils; atlas.
misconceptions: Thinking the Gulf of Mexico is an ocean: it is a gulf (part of the ocean partly surrounded by land), connected to the Atlantic.
Thinking Mexico is in South America: Mexico is in North America.

days.guide: Use a globe to find the 7 continents and 5 oceans; locate North America and the U.S.

questions.q: Name the 7 continents.
questions.a: North America, South America, Europe, Asia, Africa, Australia, Antarctica.

questions.q: Name the 5 oceans.
questions.a: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic, Southern.

days.guide: Label Canada, the U.S. and Mexico; color each; locate California.

questions.q: Which country is north of the U.S.?
questions.a: Canada.

questions.q: Which country is south of the U.S.?
questions.a: Mexico.

days.guide: Label the Pacific, Atlantic, Arctic Oceans and the Gulf of Mexico.

questions.q: Which ocean is west of California?
questions.a: The Pacific Ocean.

days.guide: Label from memory; check against an atlas; fix mistakes.

questions.q: Which ocean is north of Canada?
questions.a: The Arctic Ocean.

days.guide: Give the map quiz.

questions.q: What is a border?
questions.a: A line where one country or state ends and another begins.

weeks.assessment_key: Map quiz from memory: Canada (north), United States (middle), Mexico (south); Pacific Ocean (west), Atlantic Ocean (east), Arctic Ocean (north). Proficient = 6/6; developing = 4-5; beginning = 3 or fewer.

weeks.prep: Blank North America map, atlas, clay; blue and brown pencils.
misconceptions: Confusing the Rockies and Appalachians: the Rockies are in the west (tall, jagged); the Appalachians are in the east (older, lower, rounded).
Thinking the Mississippi flows north: it flows south to the Gulf of Mexico.

days.guide: Label the Rocky Mountains, Appalachian Mountains and Sierra Nevada; model the Rockies in clay.

questions.q: Which mountains are in eastern California?
questions.a: The Sierra Nevada.

questions.q: Which mountain range is in the eastern U.S.?
questions.a: The Appalachian Mountains.

days.guide: Trace and label the Mississippi, Missouri, Colorado and Rio Grande; discuss why rivers matter.

questions.q: Where does the Mississippi River end?
questions.a: In the Gulf of Mexico.

questions.q: Why do rivers matter to people?
questions.a: Drinking water, farming, travel and shipping, fishing, power.

days.guide: Learn the Great Lakes with HOMES; label them.

questions.q: What does HOMES stand for?
questions.a: Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie, Superior.

questions.q: Which two countries share the Great Lakes?
questions.a: The United States and Canada.

days.guide: Label the complete map from memory; check with an atlas.

questions.q: Which river forms part of the border between Texas and Mexico?
questions.a: The Rio Grande.

days.guide: Give the full map quiz.

questions.q: What is a landform?
questions.a: A natural shape of the land, like a mountain, valley or plain.

weeks.assessment_key: Map from memory: Canada, U.S., Mexico; Pacific, Atlantic, Arctic; Great Lakes (Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie, Superior); 2 rivers (e.g., Mississippi - flows south to the Gulf; Colorado - southwest, through the Grand Canyon; Missouri; Rio Grande - border of Texas and Mexico); 2 mountain ranges (Rocky - west; Appalachian - east; Sierra Nevada - eastern California). Proficient = 12+ of 15 correct.

weeks.prep: World or U.S. map, yarn and pins or stickers; family interview notes. Be sensitive if family history is unknown (adoption, etc.): the child can map the family's moves within their own lifetime instead.
misconceptions: Thinking only people from other countries are immigrants: an immigrant moves into a new country; people also migrate within a country.
Thinking people move for no reason: they move for jobs, family, safety, land or opportunity.

days.guide: Interview a family member about where ancestors lived and why they moved.

questions.q: What does migrate mean?
questions.a: To move from one place to another to live.

days.guide: Mark ancestors' homes on a map; connect to your town with yarn.

questions.q: Where did your family's journey start?
questions.a: Answer from interview.

days.guide: Learn how people traveled long ago (ship, wagon, train); draw your family's journey.

questions.q: How did many immigrants cross the ocean long ago?
questions.a: By ship.

days.guide: Discuss reasons people move; write one sentence about your family.

questions.q: Name two reasons people move.
questions.a: Jobs, to be near family, safety, land, schools, opportunity.

days.guide: Add the map to the family book; present it.

questions.q: What is an immigrant?
questions.a: A person who moves to a new country to live.

weeks.assessment_key: Migration map: ancestors' homes marked and connected to the current town; explanation gives where they came from, how they traveled, and one reason they moved (e.g., 'Great-grandpa came from Mexico by train in 1950 to find work'). Proficient = accurate map + clear reason.

weeks.prep: Calisphere photos of Los Angeles, a suburb, and a Central Valley farm; California map; chart paper.
misconceptions: Thinking rural means 'poor' or 'empty': rural areas have farms, ranches and small towns with lots of open land.
Thinking suburbs are cities: suburbs are mostly neighborhoods of houses near a city.

days.guide: Look at photos of Los Angeles, a suburb and a Central Valley farm; list land uses.

questions.q: What is the land used for in a city?
questions.a: Buildings, homes, stores, offices, roads.

questions.q: What is land used for in the Central Valley?
questions.a: Farming (crops, orchards) and ranching.

days.guide: Make a three-column chart: housing, jobs, transportation, land use.

questions.q: What is suburban?
questions.a: An area of mostly homes just outside a city.

questions.q: What is rural?
questions.a: Countryside with farms and lots of open land.

days.guide: Mark 3 urban (e.g., Los Angeles, San Francisco, San Diego), 3 suburban, 3 rural places on a California map.

questions.q: Is Los Angeles urban, suburban or rural?
questions.a: Urban.

days.guide: Decide your community type; give 3 reasons.

questions.q: Why is your community that type?
questions.a: Evidence about housing, jobs, transportation.

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 quiz.

questions.q: What does a compass rose show?
questions.a: Directions: north, south, east, west.

weeks.assessment_key: Land-use chart: Urban - apartments/tall buildings, office and store jobs, buses/trains, land mostly buildings and roads; Suburban - houses with yards, many people drive to jobs in the city, cars, land for homes, schools, shopping centers; Rural - farmhouses far apart, farming/ranching jobs, cars and trucks, land for crops and animals. Unit 2 quiz: map elements, grid squares, North America labels, land-use types correct. Proficient = chart complete + 80% quiz.

weeks.prep: Home rules chart; photos of stop and speed-limit signs; 10 sort cards; materials for a made-up game.
misconceptions: Thinking rules and laws are the same: rules are for a home, school or game; laws are made by government for everyone in a community, state or country.
Thinking rules are just to stop fun: rules keep people safe and make things fair.

days.guide: List home rules and why each exists; discuss life without them.

questions.q: Why do we have a bedtime rule?
questions.a: So you get enough sleep to be healthy.

days.guide: Walk to find signs; write the law each shows.

questions.q: What law does a stop sign show?
questions.a: Drivers must come to a full stop.

days.guide: Sort 10 examples into rules and laws.

questions.q: Is 'wear a seat belt' a rule or a law?
questions.a: A law.

questions.q: Is 'clean your room' a rule or a law?
questions.a: A rule (home rule).

days.guide: Invent a game with 3 fair rules; test them.

questions.q: What makes a rule fair?
questions.a: It applies the same way to everyone.

days.guide: Write why laws keep people safe and fair.

questions.q: What is a citizen?
questions.a: A member of a community or country with rights and responsibilities.

weeks.assessment_key: Sort: rules - bedtime at 8, wash hands before dinner, raise your hand in class, take turns in a game, no running inside; laws - stop at a stop sign, obey the speed limit, no littering, wear a seat belt, children must go to school. Written explanation: laws keep people safe (traffic laws prevent crashes) and treat people fairly (everyone follows the same laws). Proficient = 9-10 correct + both ideas.

weeks.prep: Photos of the U.S. Capitol and California State Capitol; ballot slips; a simple bill flow chart; look up your mayor's and governor's names ahead of time.
misconceptions: Thinking the president makes all laws: Congress makes federal laws; the president signs or vetoes them.
Thinking a bill is money: a bill is a written idea for a new law.

days.guide: Teach: city councils, the California State Legislature in Sacramento, and Congress in Washington, D.C., make laws.

questions.q: Where does Congress meet?
questions.a: In the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C.

questions.q: Where is California's capital?
questions.a: Sacramento.

days.guide: Follow a flow chart: idea → bill → vote → signed.

questions.q: What is a bill?
questions.a: A written idea for a new law.

questions.q: Who signs a national bill to make it law?
questions.a: The president.

days.guide: Propose, debate and vote on a 'family law.'

questions.q: What does it mean to vote?
questions.a: To make a choice that is counted with everyone else's to decide.

days.guide: Find your mayor's and governor's names; write a question.

questions.q: Who is the leader of California?
questions.a: The governor.

days.guide: Draw a lawmaking flow chart.

questions.q: What are the two parts of Congress?
questions.a: The Senate and the House of Representatives.

weeks.assessment_key: Flow chart: idea → bill written → lawmakers discuss and vote (in Congress both the House and Senate) → leader signs it (president for national laws, governor for state laws) → it becomes a law. Proficient = steps in correct order with the right lawmakers named.

weeks.prep: Photo of a courtroom; simple costumes (robe for judge); the Goldilocks story; role cards.
misconceptions: Thinking police make laws: police carry out (enforce) laws; lawmakers make them.
Thinking judges decide the punishment based on feelings: judges follow the law and the facts.

days.guide: Teach how mayors, governors, the president and police carry out laws.

questions.q: What does a police officer do?
questions.a: Enforces laws and keeps people safe.

questions.q: Who leads the country?
questions.a: The president.

days.guide: Teach how judges and juries decide whether a law was broken; view a courtroom photo.

questions.q: What does a jury do?
questions.a: A group of citizens listens to the facts and decides guilty or not guilty.

days.guide: Role-play Goldilocks' mock trial.

questions.q: What evidence shows Goldilocks was in the bears' house?
questions.a: Porridge eaten, chair broken, someone sleeping in Baby Bear's bed.

days.guide: Discuss fair consequences.

questions.q: What would be a fair consequence for Goldilocks?
questions.a: Example: apologize, fix the chair, make new porridge.

days.guide: Match roles to jobs.

questions.q: Who decides what a law means in a court?
questions.a: A judge.

weeks.assessment_key: Role matching: lawmaker - makes laws; judge - decides if a law was broken and what is fair; police officer - enforces laws and keeps people safe; president - leader of the country who carries out laws (governor - state; mayor - city); jury - group of citizens who decide guilty or not guilty. Mock trial: plays a role and uses evidence. Proficient = all matches + participation.

weeks.prep: World map; photos of Canada's Parliament and Mexico's Congress; the Preamble to the U.S. Constitution (archives.gov).
misconceptions: Thinking every country has a president: Canada's government is led by a prime minister.
Thinking 'general welfare' means money help only: it means the well-being of all the people.

days.guide: Learn Canada's Parliament makes laws; the prime minister leads; compare to Congress.

questions.q: What is Canada's lawmaking group called?
questions.a: Parliament.

questions.q: Who leads Canada's government?
questions.a: The prime minister.

days.guide: Learn Mexico's Congress and president; compare to the U.S.

questions.q: Who leads Mexico?
questions.a: A president.

questions.q: How long is a Mexican president's term?
questions.a: Six years (one term only).

days.guide: Make a chart comparing lawmakers and leaders in 3 countries.

questions.q: How are all three alike?
questions.a: All have groups of elected lawmakers and leaders chosen by voters (democracies).

days.guide: Read the Preamble; discuss 'promote the general welfare.'

questions.q: How does the Preamble begin?
questions.a: 'We the People of the United States…'

questions.q: What does 'promote the general welfare' mean?
questions.a: Help the well-being of all the people.

days.guide: Give the Unit 3 quiz.

questions.q: What is a democracy?
questions.a: A government where the people choose leaders by voting.

weeks.assessment_key: Comparison chart: U.S. - lawmakers: Congress (Senate + House); leader: president. Canada - lawmakers: Parliament (House of Commons + Senate); leader: prime minister. Mexico - lawmakers: Congress (Chamber of Deputies + Senate); leader: president. Unit 3 quiz: lawmakers make laws, president/governor/mayor and police carry them out, judges and courts decide. Proficient = chart correct + 80% quiz.

weeks.prep: 10 household items with 'Made in' labels; world map; stickers; trade-game cards (e.g., different colored cards per player).
misconceptions: Thinking imports and exports are the same: imports come into a country; exports are sent out.
Thinking a country can make everything it needs: climate, land and skills differ, so nations trade.

days.guide: Find where 10 household items were made; mark countries on a map.

questions.q: Which country made the most items in our house?
questions.a: Answer from labels (often China or the U.S.).

days.guide: Learn nations trade for what they can't make or grow: bananas from Central America; almonds exported from California.

questions.q: Why does the U.S. import bananas?
questions.a: Bananas need a warm, tropical climate, so most are grown in Central and South America.

questions.q: What is an export?
questions.a: A good sent out of a country to sell.

days.guide: Play a trading game to complete sets.

questions.q: Why did you need to trade?
questions.a: You didn't have all the goods you needed.

days.guide: Read about California exports (almonds, movies, technology).

questions.q: Name a California export.
questions.a: Almonds, movies, technology, wine, dairy.

days.guide: Write 3 sentences about why trade helps nations.

questions.q: What is an import?
questions.a: A good brought into a country from another.

weeks.assessment_key: Trade map: countries from 10 labels marked correctly. Written sentences (any 3 accurate): nations trade to get goods they can't make or grow (bananas grow in warm Central America); trade lets nations sell what they make well (California almonds); trade gives people more choices and jobs; trade helps nations work together. Proficient = accurate map + 3 sentences.

weeks.prep: Library of Congress photo of the 1912 cherry tree planting in Washington, D.C.; Peace Arch photos; paper for a 'treaty.'
misconceptions: Thinking a treaty is a gift: a treaty is a written agreement between nations.
Thinking cultures only share by trade: also through gifts, music, food, games and visits.

days.guide: Study the 1912 cherry tree photo; discuss gifts between nations.

questions.q: Which country gave the cherry trees?
questions.a: Japan (the city of Tokyo).

questions.q: Why do nations give gifts?
questions.a: To show friendship and build good relations.

days.guide: Learn about the Peace Arch on the U.S.-Canada border (Washington State and British Columbia).

questions.q: What does the Peace Arch stand for?
questions.a: Peace and friendship between the United States and Canada.

days.guide: Learn that a treaty is an agreement; write a toy-sharing 'treaty' with a sibling.

questions.q: What is a treaty?
questions.a: A written agreement between nations.

days.guide: Learn and share a song, food or game from another country.

questions.q: What is culture?
questions.a: The way of life of a group: food, language, music, holidays, beliefs.

days.guide: Explain one way nations share culture and one way they make agreements.

questions.q: Give an example of sharing culture.
questions.a: Japan giving cherry trees; sharing music or food.

weeks.assessment_key: Primary source analysis: identifies who (Japan gave, U.S. received; First Lady Helen Taft helped plant the first trees in 1912), what (cherry trees), why (a gift of friendship). Peace Arch: symbol of peace and friendship between the U.S. and Canada. Treaty: written agreement with terms both siblings sign. Proficient = all.

weeks.prep: Photo of United Nations headquarters (New York) and of the 1945 Charter signing in San Francisco; problem scenario cards.
misconceptions: Thinking the UN is a country: it is an organization where many countries meet to work for peace.
Thinking conflicts must end with a winner: diplomacy looks for solutions both sides accept.

days.guide: Teach that diplomats talk to solve problems; role-play a water-sharing problem.

questions.q: What is diplomacy?
questions.a: Talking and working out agreements to solve problems between nations.

days.guide: Learn the UN was founded in San Francisco in 1945; look at the signing photo.

questions.q: Where was the UN Charter signed?
questions.a: San Francisco, California, in 1945.

questions.q: Why was the UN created?
questions.a: To help countries keep peace and work together after World War II.

days.guide: Practice peaceful problem-solving steps with scenarios.

questions.q: What are the peaceful problem-solving steps?
questions.a: Calm down, say the problem, listen, think of solutions, agree on one.

days.guide: Discuss that sometimes nations use military force and why peace is preferred.

questions.q: Why is peace better than fighting?
questions.a: People stay safe, and nations can trade and work together.

days.guide: Give the Unit 4 quiz.

questions.q: What is a conflict?
questions.a: A disagreement or fight.

weeks.assessment_key: Role-play: two 'countries' share water fairly by talking (state the problem, listen, offer ideas, agree). Unit 4 quiz: trade (imports/exports), cultural contact (cherry tree gift), treaty (agreement between nations), diplomacy (talking to solve problems), UN founded 1945 in San Francisco. Proficient = peaceful solution reached + 80% quiz.

weeks.prep: 12 picture cards (bread, shoes, apple, toy, book, bike; haircut, doctor visit, teaching, bus ride, mail delivery, car repair); play money; web paper.
misconceptions: Thinking a person is only a producer or only a consumer: everyone is a consumer, and workers are also producers.
Thinking services aren't 'real' because you can't hold them: services are work people do for others.

days.guide: Sort 12 cards into goods and services.

questions.q: What are goods?
questions.a: Things you can buy and hold.

questions.q: What are services?
questions.a: Work people do for others.

days.guide: Interview a family member: goods or services at work?

questions.q: Does a teacher provide goods or a service?
questions.a: A service.

days.guide: List family purchases this week; label goods or services.

questions.q: What is a consumer?
questions.a: A person who buys or uses goods and services.

days.guide: Draw a web of how a baker depends on others.

questions.q: Who does the baker depend on for flour?
questions.a: Farmers who grow wheat and mills that grind it.

days.guide: Write 3 sentences about how buyers and sellers need each other.

questions.q: What is a producer?
questions.a: A person who makes goods or provides services.

weeks.assessment_key: Sort: goods - bread, shoes, apple, toy, book, bike; services - haircut, doctor visit, teaching, bus ride, mail delivery, car repair. Interdependence web: baker linked to farmer (wheat), miller (flour), truck driver (delivery), customers (buy bread), store. Proficient = 12/12 + web with 3+ links.

weeks.prep: Milk carton, cereal box, flowchart paper; plan a grocery visit.
misconceptions: Thinking the store makes food: the store sells food grown and processed by others.
Leaving out transportation: trucks and trains carry food at many steps.

days.guide: Trace milk from cow to fridge; draw the flowchart.

questions.q: What happens at the dairy processing plant?
questions.a: Milk is heated (pasteurized), packaged and cooled.

days.guide: Trace cereal from wheat field to factory to store.

questions.q: What grain is in many cereals?
questions.a: Wheat, oats, corn or rice.

days.guide: Visit a grocery store; find 5 foods grown in California.

questions.q: Name a food grown in California.
questions.a: Strawberries, almonds, lettuce, oranges, grapes, tomatoes, avocados.

days.guide: Match food jobs: farmer, processor, distributor, grocer.

questions.q: What does a distributor do?
questions.a: Moves food from farms and factories to stores.

questions.q: What does a processor do?
questions.a: Turns raw food into products (cleans, cooks, packages).

days.guide: Explain farm-to-table steps for one food.

questions.q: Who grows the food?
questions.a: Farmers.

weeks.assessment_key: Flowchart for milk: cow on dairy farm → milked → truck → processing plant (pasteurized, bottled) → distributor truck → grocery store → home fridge. Cereal: wheat field (farmer) → mill/factory (processor) → truck (distributor) → store (grocer) → home. Proficient = 5+ steps in order with workers named.

weeks.prep: Calisphere photos of early-1900s California farms and modern farm photos; apples and an oven or dehydrator (adult help); Venn diagram paper.
misconceptions: Thinking farms long ago had tractors like today: many used horses, mules and hand tools.
Thinking preserving means freezing: long ago people canned, dried, salted and smoked food.

days.guide: Look at early California farm photos; list tools and animals.

questions.q: What pulled plows long ago?
questions.a: Horses or mules.

days.guide: Compare with modern farm photos.

questions.q: What machine replaced horses on farms?
questions.a: Tractors.

questions.q: What is irrigation?
questions.a: Bringing water to crops through canals, pipes or sprinklers.

days.guide: Ask a grandparent how food was bought and cooked when young.

questions.q: What did you learn?
questions.a: Fact from interview.

days.guide: Learn canning and drying; make dried apple slices with an adult.

questions.q: Why did people preserve food long ago?
questions.a: To keep food from spoiling so they had food in winter.

questions.q: What does drying do?
questions.a: Removes water so germs can't grow.

days.guide: Venn diagram of food production long ago and today.

questions.q: How is farming the same today?
questions.a: Farmers still need soil, water and sun to grow crops.

weeks.assessment_key: Venn diagram: Long ago - horses/mules, hand tools, more people working each farm, canning/drying at home, food grown closer to home; Today - tractors and machines, sprinkler/drip irrigation, refrigerated trucks, supermarkets; Both - farmers grow food, need water, sun and soil, harvest crops. Proficient = 2+ accurate items in each section.

weeks.prep: California physical map; Calisphere photos of the California Aqueduct; bean seeds, 2 cups, soil; a short article on a California drought.
misconceptions: Thinking weather only affects farmers: it changes how much food is in stores and its price.
Thinking California has plenty of rain everywhere: much farm water comes from Sierra snowmelt carried by canals and aqueducts.

days.guide: Read frost, rain and heat-wave scenarios; tell how each changes food sales.

questions.q: What could a frost do to orange trees?
questions.a: Freeze and damage the oranges, so farmers have fewer to sell.

days.guide: Look at the California Aqueduct photos; trace how Sierra snowmelt reaches farms.

questions.q: Where does much of California's farm water come from?
questions.a: Melting snow in the Sierra Nevada, carried by rivers, aqueducts and canals.

questions.q: What is an aqueduct?
questions.a: A large channel or pipe that carries water a long way.

days.guide: Plant beans in two cups (plenty vs. little water); record twice.

questions.q: Which bean will grow better?
questions.a: The one with plenty of water.

days.guide: Read about a California drought; discuss farmers' choices.

questions.q: What is a drought?
questions.a: A long time with much less rain or snow than normal.

questions.q: Why did some farmers leave fields empty?
questions.a: There wasn't enough water to grow crops there.

days.guide: Write 3 sentences on weather, land, water and food.

questions.q: What is a resource?
questions.a: Something people use, like water, land or trees.

weeks.assessment_key: Three sentences (accurate examples): 1) Bad weather like frost, heavy rain or heat waves can ruin crops, so there is less food to sell and prices go up. 2) Farmers need good land (flat, rich soil) like the Central Valley to grow lots of food. 3) Water from Sierra snowmelt travels through rivers, aqueducts and canals to irrigate farms; in a drought, farmers grow less. Proficient = all three factors linked to food.

weeks.prep: Crackers, play money, a pretend restaurant menu, grid paper (20 squares) for a farm, a family grocery list and budget.
misconceptions: Thinking scarcity only means 'none': scarcity means not enough for everyone's wants.
Thinking a choice costs nothing: every choice has a trade-off: what you give up.

days.guide: Share 5 crackers among 7 people; define scarcity.

questions.q: What is scarcity?
questions.a: Not having enough of something for everyone who wants it.

days.guide: Order from a menu with $10; write what was chosen and given up.

questions.q: If you spend $7 on pizza, how much is left from $10?
What is a trade-off?
questions.a: What you give up when you make a choice.

days.guide: Plan a 20-square farm; divide among crops; explain.

questions.q: If you plant 8 squares of almonds and 7 of tomatoes, how many for lettuce?
questions.a: 5 squares.

days.guide: Plan a real grocery list within a budget; cross out wants.

questions.q: What is the difference between a need and a want?
questions.a: A need is necessary to live (food, water); a want is nice to have.

days.guide: Write about one choice and its trade-off.

questions.q: Why do people have to make choices?
questions.a: Resources like money and time are limited.

weeks.assessment_key: Trade-off explanations name the choice, what was given up, and why (e.g., 'I bought a burger for $6 and lemonade for $4, so I gave up the $3 dessert because I was hungrier for the meal'). Grid farm: 20 squares divided among almonds, tomatoes, lettuce with a reason tied to limited land/water (almonds need water year-round). Proficient = clear trade-offs + reasoned plan.

weeks.prep: Play money; materials for 5 items to sell (bookmarks, drawings); price tags and a sign.
misconceptions: Thinking barter is easy: both people must want what the other has.
Thinking profit is all the money you collect: profit is what is left after paying your costs.

days.guide: Try bartering; record problems.

questions.q: What is barter?
questions.a: Trading goods or services without money.

questions.q: What problem can happen with barter?
questions.a: The other person may not want what you have.

days.guide: Read how people used shells, salt and coins; explain how money helps.

questions.q: How does money solve barter problems?
questions.a: Everyone accepts money, so you can buy what you want from anyone.

days.guide: Make 5 items, set prices, make a sign.

questions.q: How do you decide a price?
questions.a: Think about cost to make it and what buyers will pay.

days.guide: Run a family market; buy and sell; record sales.

questions.q: If you sell 4 bookmarks for $2 each, how much do you earn?

days.guide: Write 3 sentences: produced, consumed, needed each other.

questions.q: What is a market?
questions.a: A place where people buy and sell goods.

weeks.assessment_key: Sales record: items sold, prices, total money (e.g., 3 bookmarks × $1 + 2 drawings × $2 = $7). Reflection: what they produced (bookmarks), what they consumed (bought a snack), and how buyers and sellers needed each other (seller needs buyers' money; buyer wants seller's goods). Proficient = accurate math + all three ideas.

weeks.prep: Poster paper, food packaging, Calisphere and library sources; California map.
misconceptions: Using only one source: check facts in 2 sources.
Leaving out workers: name the person doing each step.

days.guide: Choose a food; find where it's grown in California.

questions.q: Where are many strawberries grown in California?
questions.a: Coastal areas like Watsonville/Salinas and Oxnard/Santa Maria.

days.guide: Use 2 sources to research growers, processors, transport, sellers, weather and water.

questions.q: Why use 2 sources?
questions.a: To check that facts are correct.

days.guide: Make a 5-step poster with map and worker labels.

questions.q: What is the first step for your food?
questions.a: Growing it on a farm.

days.guide: Present; explain one difference between long ago and today.

questions.q: How is your food grown differently today?
questions.a: Machines, irrigation, refrigerated trucks.

days.guide: Give the Unit 5 quiz.

questions.q: Is a farmer a producer or consumer?
questions.a: Both: a producer of food, and a consumer when buying things.

weeks.assessment_key: Poster: 5 steps in order (grow, harvest, process, transport, sell), California map marking where it's grown, labels for each worker, weather/water needs, and one long-ago vs. today difference (e.g., 'strawberries were picked and carried by hand; now trucks with refrigeration get them to stores fast'). Unit 5 quiz: goods vs. services, producer vs. consumer, farm-to-table order, scarcity choice. Proficient = complete poster + 80% quiz.

weeks.prep: Picture-book biography of Abraham Lincoln (library); copies of Grace Bedell's 1860 letter and Lincoln's reply (available online from library and archive collections); a penny and five-dollar bill; Lincoln Memorial photo.
misconceptions: Thinking heroes are only superheroes or famous people: heroes are people who show traits like courage and kindness to help others.
Thinking Lincoln grew up rich and went to fancy schools: he grew up poor and mostly taught himself.

days.guide: List admired people and their traits; make a hero-traits chart.

questions.q: What is a character trait?
questions.a: A quality that describes how a person acts, like honest or brave.

questions.q: Name two hero traits.
questions.a: Courage, honesty, kindness, perseverance.

days.guide: Read a Lincoln biography; put 5 events on a timeline.

questions.q: Where was Lincoln born?
questions.a: In a log cabin in Kentucky.

questions.q: What number president was Lincoln?
questions.a: The 16th president.

days.guide: Read Grace Bedell's letter (she suggested a beard because his face was thin) and Lincoln's reply.

questions.q: How old was Grace Bedell?
questions.a: 11 years old.

questions.q: What does it show that Lincoln answered her?
questions.a: He listened to ordinary people, even children.

days.guide: Look at Lincoln on the penny, $5 bill and Lincoln Memorial; discuss traits.

questions.q: Why is Lincoln honored?
questions.a: He kept the nation together during the Civil War and worked to end slavery.

questions.q: What nickname shows a trait?
questions.a: 'Honest Abe' (honesty).

days.guide: Write a letter to a leader with one idea and a reason.

questions.q: What parts does a letter need?
questions.a: Date, greeting, body, closing, signature.

weeks.assessment_key: Timeline in order: born in a log cabin in Kentucky (1809) → taught himself to read → became a lawyer in Illinois → elected 16th president (1860) → led the nation in the Civil War and worked to end slavery (Emancipation Proclamation 1863, 13th Amendment). Letter to a leader: greeting, one idea, a reason, closing and signature. Proficient = correct order + complete letter.

weeks.prep: Biographies of Sitting Bull and George Washington Carver; Library of Congress photos of Sitting Bull and of Carver at Tuskegee Institute; peanuts and sweet potatoes (check for peanut allergy; skip tasting if needed).
misconceptions: Believing Carver invented peanut butter: peanut butter existed before him; he developed many other uses for peanuts and sweet potatoes and taught crop rotation.
Thinking Sitting Bull fought for no reason: he defended his people's land and way of life when the U.S. government broke promises and took Lakota lands.

days.guide: Read a Sitting Bull biography; discuss protecting land and way of life.

questions.q: Who was Sitting Bull?
questions.a: A Hunkpapa Lakota (Sioux) leader and holy man.

questions.q: What did he work to protect?
questions.a: His people's land, buffalo hunting and way of life.

days.guide: Study a Sitting Bull photo: see, wonder, learn.

questions.q: What can a photo tell us?
questions.a: How he looked and dressed, and clues about his time.

days.guide: Read a Carver biography; learn crop rotation with peanuts.

questions.q: Why did farmers' soil wear out?
questions.a: Planting cotton year after year used up nutrients.

questions.q: How did peanuts help?
questions.a: Peanuts put nutrients (nitrogen) back into the soil.

days.guide: Look at Carver's products; taste peanuts and sweet potatoes if safe; view his lab photo.

questions.q: Name products Carver made from peanuts.
questions.a: Dyes, paints, cosmetics, cooking oils, and many more (hundreds of uses).

days.guide: Complete hero-traits charts with evidence.

questions.q: Which trait did Carver show and how?
questions.a: Perseverance: he was born into slavery but kept learning and became a scientist.

weeks.assessment_key: Hero-traits chart with evidence: Sitting Bull - courage, leadership, loyalty (led the Hunkpapa Lakota, refused to give up their land and way of life, a leader at the Battle of the Little Bighorn in 1876). Carver - perseverance, curiosity, helpfulness (born into slavery, worked hard for an education, taught farmers to rotate crops with peanuts and sweet potatoes to restore the soil, found hundreds of uses for them). Proficient = 2 traits each with accurate evidence.

weeks.prep: Milk or juice carton labeled 'pasteurized'; biographies of Louis Pasteur and Marie Curie; photo of Curie in her lab; 2 bread slices and a zip bag (keep the moldy slice sealed and don't sniff it; discard after).
misconceptions: Thinking pasteurization adds chemicals: it heats milk or juice to kill harmful germs.
Thinking women couldn't be scientists then: they faced unfair barriers, and Marie Curie succeeded anyway.

days.guide: Read about Pasteur; find 'pasteurized' on a carton; explain heating kills germs.

questions.q: What does pasteurized mean?
questions.a: Heated to kill harmful germs.

questions.q: What country was Pasteur from?
questions.a: France.

days.guide: Leave one bread slice out and seal another; observe mold.

questions.q: What is mold?
questions.a: A fungus that grows on food, especially when it's left out.

questions.q: How does this connect to Pasteur?
questions.a: He showed tiny living things (germs) make food spoil.

days.guide: Read about Marie Curie's two Nobel Prizes.

questions.q: What was special about Marie Curie's Nobel Prizes?
questions.a: She was the first woman to win one and the first person to win two (physics 1903, chemistry 1911).

days.guide: Look at Curie's lab photo; discuss perseverance.

questions.q: What is perseverance?
questions.a: Keeping on even when things are hard.

days.guide: Write how Pasteur and Curie made a difference.

questions.q: How does Pasteur help you today?
questions.a: Pasteurized milk is safe to drink; vaccines prevent diseases.

weeks.assessment_key: Written comparison (2 sentences each): Pasteur - showed that germs cause food to spoil and people to get sick; invented pasteurization so milk and juice are safe today, and made vaccines (like the rabies vaccine). Curie - discovered radium and polonium and studied radioactivity; her work helped lead to X-rays and cancer treatments; first woman to win a Nobel Prize and first person to win two. Proficient = accurate contribution for each with a today connection.

weeks.prep: 'On a Beam of Light' by Jennifer Berne (Einstein); a biography of Golda Meir; world map.
misconceptions: Thinking Einstein was always a top student: he was curious and asked big questions, and sometimes struggled in strict schools.
Thinking immigrants stay in one place: Golda Meir moved from Ukraine to the U.S. and later to Israel.

days.guide: Read 'On a Beam of Light'; list Einstein's childhood questions.

questions.q: What object made young Einstein curious?
questions.a: A compass (the needle always pointed north).

questions.q: What did he imagine?
questions.a: Riding on a beam of light.

days.guide: Write 3 'I wonder' questions; choose one to investigate.

questions.q: What is curiosity?
questions.a: Wanting to know and learn about things.

days.guide: Read about Golda Meir; locate Ukraine, the U.S. and Israel.

questions.q: What job did Golda Meir have in the U.S.?
questions.a: Teacher.

questions.q: What did she become?
questions.a: Prime minister of Israel.

days.guide: Make a Venn diagram comparing Einstein and Meir.

questions.q: How are Einstein and Meir alike?
questions.a: Both were immigrants who made a difference.

days.guide: Add both to the hero timeline; name traits.

questions.q: Which trait did Einstein show most?
questions.a: Curiosity and imagination.

weeks.assessment_key: Venn diagram: Einstein - scientist, born in Germany, asked questions about light, time and space, won Nobel Prize; Meir - teacher and leader, born in Ukraine, grew up in Milwaukee, became prime minister of Israel; Both - immigrants who moved to new countries, worked hard, made a difference. Traits: Einstein - curiosity/imagination; Meir - leadership/determination. Proficient = accurate Venn + trait each.

weeks.prep: 'Teammates' by Peter Golenbock; Jackie Robinson's 1958 letter to President Eisenhower (DocsTeach/National Archives); baseball and glove; poster paper.
misconceptions: Thinking segregation was just a rule of baseball: it was unfair separation of people by race in many parts of life.
Thinking staying calm meant Jackie didn't care: it took great courage and self-control not to fight back.

days.guide: Read 'Teammates'; discuss courage of Jackie Robinson and Pee Wee Reese in 1947.

questions.q: What team did Jackie Robinson join in 1947?
questions.a: The Brooklyn Dodgers.

questions.q: What did Pee Wee Reese do?
questions.a: In front of a booing crowd, he put his arm around Jackie to show he was his teammate.

days.guide: Teach segregation and why it was unfair; discuss staying calm.

questions.q: What is segregation?
questions.a: Keeping people apart because of their race.

questions.q: Why did Jackie promise not to fight back?
questions.a: Branch Rickey asked him to stay calm so people would focus on his talent and the cause.

days.guide: Read parts of the 1958 letter to Eisenhower.

questions.q: What did Jackie ask President Eisenhower?
questions.a: Not to tell Black Americans to be patient, but to act to protect their equal rights now.

days.guide: Play catch; learn #42 is retired by every MLB team; design a Jackie Robinson Day poster.

questions.q: What number did Jackie wear?
When is Jackie Robinson Day?
questions.a: April 15 (the date of his first major league game in 1947).

days.guide: Write how Jackie made a difference, with a letter detail.

questions.q: What is the 'color barrier'?
questions.a: The unfair rule that kept Black players out of Major League Baseball.

weeks.assessment_key: Written response: Jackie Robinson broke Major League Baseball's color barrier in 1947 with the Brooklyn Dodgers, showing courage that opened the way for other Black players; in his 1958 letter he told President Eisenhower that Black Americans should not have to keep waiting patiently and asked him to act now to protect equal rights. Proficient = accurate contribution + detail from the letter.

weeks.prep: Rosa Parks' police record (National Archives); an excerpt of Dr. King's 'I Have a Dream' speech (1963); 'The Story of Ruby Bridges' by Robert Coles; hero timeline. Preview to explain unfair laws calmly.
misconceptions: Thinking Rosa Parks was simply tired: she was tired of unfair treatment and chose to stand up for equal rights.
Thinking civil rights leaders used violence: they used peaceful protest like boycotts, marches and speeches.

days.guide: Read about Rosa Parks; view her police record; discuss courage.

questions.q: What did Rosa Parks do in 1955?
questions.a: Refused to give up her bus seat to a white man in Montgomery, Alabama, and was arrested.

questions.q: What happened next?
questions.a: Black residents boycotted Montgomery's buses for over a year until the buses were desegregated.

days.guide: Listen to 'I Have a Dream'; write your own dream.

questions.q: What was Dr. King's dream?
questions.a: That his children would be judged by the content of their character, not the color of their skin.

days.guide: Read 'The Story of Ruby Bridges'; discuss.

questions.q: How old was Ruby Bridges?
questions.a: 6 years old.

questions.q: What did Ruby do when crowds shouted at her?
questions.a: She stayed brave, walked into school with federal marshals, and prayed for the people shouting.

days.guide: Place 1947, 1955, 1960, 1963 on the timeline.

questions.q: Which came first: the bus boycott or Ruby Bridges?
questions.a: The bus boycott (1955), before Ruby Bridges (1960).

days.guide: Explain how each used peaceful action.

questions.q: What is a boycott?
questions.a: Refusing to buy or use something to protest unfairness.

weeks.assessment_key: Timeline: 1947 Jackie Robinson joins the Dodgers; 1955 Montgomery Bus Boycott begins after Rosa Parks' arrest; 1960 Ruby Bridges integrates William Frantz Elementary in New Orleans; 1963 March on Washington and 'I Have a Dream.' Explanation: Parks peacefully refused to give up her bus seat, leading to a boycott; King led peaceful marches and gave speeches; Ruby bravely went to school each day despite angry crowds. Proficient = correct order + peaceful action for each.

weeks.prep: 'Harvesting Hope: The Story of Cesar Chavez' by Kathleen Krull; Calisphere photos of the 1966 Delano-to-Sacramento march; California map.
misconceptions: Thinking Chavez worked alone: he co-founded the farmworkers' union with Dolores Huerta and thousands joined.
Thinking a union is a company: a union is a group of workers joining together to ask for fair pay and safe conditions.

days.guide: Read 'Harvesting Hope'; discuss farmworkers' lives and why Chavez organized.

questions.q: What was life like for farmworkers?
questions.a: Long, hard hours in the fields for very low pay, poor housing, and unsafe conditions.

questions.q: Why did Chavez organize workers?
questions.a: So together they could ask for fair pay and better treatment.

days.guide: Trace the 1966 march from Delano to Sacramento; view photos.

questions.q: Why march to Sacramento?
questions.a: It's the state capital, where they could ask leaders to listen.

questions.q: About how far was the march?
questions.a: About 300 miles.

days.guide: Read about Dolores Huerta and 'Sí, se puede.'

questions.q: What does 'Sí, se puede' mean?
questions.a: Yes, we can (yes, it can be done).

days.guide: Connect to farm-to-table: who picks grapes and lettuce?

questions.q: Who picks much of the fruit and vegetables we buy?
questions.a: Farmworkers.

days.guide: Write a paragraph on how Chavez and Huerta made a difference.

questions.q: What is nonviolence?
questions.a: Working for change without hurting anyone.

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph: Chavez and Huerta organized farmworkers into a union (National Farm Workers Association, later the United Farm Workers) to win fair pay, safer conditions and respect, using nonviolent actions like strikes, the grape boycott and the 1966 march from Delano to Sacramento; Huerta's motto 'Sí, se puede' gave hope. Map: Delano (southern San Joaquin Valley) to Sacramento, about 300 miles north. Proficient = accurate paragraph + correct route.

weeks.prep: NASA photo of Sally Ride on STS-7 (1983); biographies of Sally Ride and Ellen Ochoa; straws, paper and tape for paper rockets.
misconceptions: Thinking astronauts are only pilots: many are scientists and engineers.
Thinking only boys can become astronauts: Ride and Ochoa showed girls can too.

days.guide: Read about Sally Ride; study the NASA photo.

questions.q: Who was the first American woman in space?
questions.a: Sally Ride, in 1983.

questions.q: What was the space shuttle she flew on?
questions.a: Challenger (mission STS-7).

days.guide: Read about Ellen Ochoa.

questions.q: What 'first' did Ellen Ochoa achieve?
questions.a: First Hispanic woman in space (1993).

questions.q: What job did she have later?
questions.a: Director of NASA's Johnson Space Center.

days.guide: Build and launch straw paper rockets.

questions.q: What is an engineer?
questions.a: Someone who designs and builds things to solve problems.

days.guide: Discuss Sally Ride's science programs for girls; write how you could inspire someone.

questions.q: How did Sally Ride inspire others?
questions.a: She started programs and wrote books to get kids, especially girls, excited about science.

days.guide: Add both astronauts to the hero timeline and traits chart.

questions.q: What is NASA?
questions.a: The U.S. space agency.

weeks.assessment_key: Traits chart: Sally Ride - courage, curiosity, inspiring others (first American woman in space in 1983 on the shuttle Challenger; physicist from Los Angeles; started Sally Ride Science for kids). Ellen Ochoa - perseverance, intelligence, leadership (from La Mesa, CA; first Hispanic woman in space in 1993; engineer/inventor; flew 4 missions; later director of Johnson Space Center). Timeline entries 1983 and 1993. Proficient = accurate traits and dates.

weeks.prep: Interview questions; phone; card supplies; a short biography of Fred Korematsu (e.g., 'Fred Korematsu Speaks Up'). Preview: explain simply that during World War II the government unfairly forced Japanese Americans to leave their homes and live in camps.
misconceptions: Thinking heroes must be famous: everyday people who help others are heroes too.
Thinking Korematsu lost so he failed: decades later his conviction was overturned and he is honored for standing up for fairness.

days.guide: Brainstorm community heroes.

questions.q: Name a community helper who makes a difference.
questions.a: Firefighter, librarian, volunteer, coach, nurse.

days.guide: Interview a community helper with 5 questions.

questions.q: What is a volunteer?
questions.a: Someone who helps others without being paid.

days.guide: Read about Fred Korematsu.

questions.q: What did Fred Korematsu stand up against?
questions.a: The unfair order forcing Japanese Americans into camps during World War II.

questions.q: When is Fred Korematsu Day?
questions.a: January 30.

days.guide: Plan and do one helpful act.

questions.q: What helpful act did you do?
questions.a: Describes act.

days.guide: Write a thank-you card naming an admired trait.

questions.q: What trait did your helper show?
questions.a: Example: kindness, dedication, generosity.

weeks.assessment_key: Interview notes with 5 questions and answers; one service act completed and described; thank-you card names a trait (e.g., 'Thank you for being generous with your time at the food bank').
